answers.question: If we double the length and width of a MOSFET, what happens to its intrinsic gain?

answer.text:
The intrinsic gain of a MOSFET is \(A_v=g_m r_o\).

With fixed bias voltages (hence fixed overdrive), doubling both \(W\) and \(L\) leaves the ratio \(W/L\) unchanged. Consequently both \(I_D\) and \(g_m\) are unchanged. Because the channel-length modulation parameter satisfies \(\lambda\propto 1/L\), doubling \(L\) halves \(\lambda\). With \(I_D\) constant this doubles \(r_o\).

Therefore \(A_v\) doubles. (Equivalently, \(A_v\propto L/V_{ov}\) at constant overdrive, so the same factor-of-two increase is obtained.)

Final answer: doubles

answers.question: Student A says the transconductance of a MOSFET goes up as the overdrive voltage increases. Student B says it goes down. Who is correct?

answer.text:
The MOSFET transconductance in saturation is obtained by differentiating the square-law drain current with respect to gate-source voltage (device dimensions fixed):

\[
g_m=\mu C_{\rm ox}\frac{W}{L}V_{\rm ov}.
\]

Thus \(g_m\) rises linearly with overdrive. (The same conclusion follows from \(g_m=\sqrt{2\mu C_{\rm ox}(W/L)I_D}\) once it is recognized that \(I_D\) itself grows as \(V_{\rm ov}^2\).)

The inverse dependence \(g_m=2I_D/V_{\rm ov}\) appears only when current is held constant while \(W/L\) is changed; that is a different experiment from simply raising the overdrive of a given MOSFET. Secondary effects (mobility degradation, velocity saturation) can eventually flatten or weakly reduce \(g_m\), but they do not reverse the first-order result that Student A states.

Final answer: Student A

answers.question: Is the small-signal model of a PMOS device identical to that of an NMOS device?

answer.text:
The small-signal models are identical. Although the large-signal polarities of \(V_{GS}\), \(V_{DS}\) and \(I_D\) are reversed for a PMOS device, the partial derivatives that define the small-signal parameters (\(g_m\), \(g_{mb}\), \(r_o\), and the various capacitances) produce exactly the same controlled-source topology and element relationships used for an NMOS device.

Final answer: yes

answers.question: Is the small-signal model of a PMOS device identical to that of an NMOS device?

answer.text:
The basic low-frequency small-signal (hybrid-\(\pi\)) model of a MOSFET consists of a voltage-controlled current source \(g_m v_{gs}\) in parallel with the output resistance \(r_o\).  

Because all small-signal quantities are defined as incremental deviations from the DC bias point, the same controlled-source topology and the same parameter definitions (\(g_m>0\), \(r_o>0\)) apply to both device polarities. Consequently the small-signal model of a PMOS transistor is identical to that of an NMOS transistor (body effect, capacitances, etc., may be added in exactly the same way for either device).

Final answer: yes

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The figure shows a single MOSFET stage: gate driven by \(V_{in}\), upper device terminal tied to \(V_{DD}\) through \(R_S\), lower terminal tied to ground through \(R_D\), with \(V_{out}\) taken at the lower terminal.

## Terminals and polarity
The source arrow is drawn on the upper terminal and points into the channel, so \(M_1\) is an NMOS with:
- source = upper terminal (through \(R_S\) to \(V_{DD}\))
- drain = lower terminal (\(V_{out}\), through \(R_D\) to ground)
- gate = \(V_{in}\)

Input at the gate and output at the drain makes this nominally a common-source stage with source degeneration \(R_S\).

## The problem with this orientation
In the three-terminal symbol the body is tied to the source. For an NMOS the body–drain junction is a diode with its anode at the source/body node and its cathode at the drain. Here the source sits up toward \(V_{DD}\) and the drain sits down toward ground, so that diode is forward biased and clamps

\[
V_S - V_D \approx 0.7\,\text{V}.
\]

The channel is then shunted by the diode, and the current is set by the resistors rather than by the gate:

\[
I \approx \frac{V_{DD}-0.7}{R_S+R_D}, \qquad V_{out}=I\,R_D,
\]

essentially independent of \(V_{in}\). As drawn, the circuit does not operate as a gate-controlled amplifier. An NMOS only works as a common-source amplifier with the drain as the higher-potential terminal (drain resistor up to \(V_{DD}\), source resistor down to ground), so the body diode stays reverse biased.

## If it is meant as a working amplifier
The same topology functions if the device is a PMOS (source toward \(V_{DD}\), drain toward ground), which is the polarity consistent with the resistor labels \(R_S\) on top and \(R_D\) on the bottom. Treating it that way, in saturation with the body at the source (no body effect) and neglecting \(r_o\):

\[
v_{in}=v_{gs}(1+g_m R_S), \qquad i_d=\frac{g_m}{1+g_m R_S}v_{in},
\]

\[
A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=-\frac{g_m R_D}{1+g_m R_S}.
\]

It is an inverting stage; \(R_S\) degenerates the gain (and raises linearity and input range), and the gain approaches \(-R_D/R_S\) for \(g_m R_S \gg 1\). With finite \(r_o\) the magnitude is somewhat smaller, and if the body is not at the source the denominator becomes \(1+(g_m+g_{mb})R_S\).

For the PMOS reading, saturation requires \(V_{SD}\ge V_{SG}-|V_{tp}|\), i.e. \(V_{out}\le V_{in}+|V_{tp}|\), with the bias current set implicitly by \(I=\tfrac12 k_p'(W/L)(V_{DD}-IR_S-V_{in}-|V_{tp}|)^2\).

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The circuit is a **PMOS common-source amplifier with source degeneration**.

### Identification
- \(M_1\) is a **p-channel MOSFET**: the source arrow points into the channel, and the source resistor \(R_S\) sits on the \(V_{DD}\) side while the drain resistor \(R_D\) returns to ground.
- Gate = input \(V_{\text{in}}\)
- Source → \(R_S\) → \(V_{DD}\)
- Drain → \(V_{\text{out}}\), with \(R_D\) to ground
- The 3-terminal symbol implies the body is taken as tied to the source (no body effect), unless an IC well tie to \(V_{DD}\) is assumed.

### Large-signal behavior
Current flows \(V_{DD}\to R_S\to\) source \(\to\) drain \(\to R_D\to\) ground, so
\[
V_S=V_{DD}-I_DR_S,\qquad V_D=V_{\text{out}}=I_DR_D.
\]
In saturation,
\[
I_D=\frac12\mu_pC_{\text{ox}}\frac{W}{L}\bigl(V_{SG}-|V_{tp}|\bigr)^2,
\]
which requires
\[
V_{SG}>|V_{tp}|\quad\Rightarrow\quad V_{\text{in}}<V_S-|V_{tp}|
\]
and
\[
V_{SD}\ge V_{SG}-|V_{tp}|\quad\Rightarrow\quad V_{\text{out}}\le V_{\text{in}}+|V_{tp}|.
\]
Raising \(V_{\text{in}}\) reduces \(V_{SG}\), so \(I_D\) and \(V_{\text{out}}\) both fall: the stage **inverts**.

### Small-signal gain
With \(g_m=\partial I_D/\partial V_{SG}\) and neglecting \(r_o\) and body effect,
\[
A_v=\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{v_{\text{in}}}=-\frac{g_mR_D}{1+g_mR_S}.
\]
\(R_S\) is unbypassed source degeneration: it lowers \(|A_v|\) by \(1+g_mR_S\) and linearizes the gain. If \(R_S=0\), this reduces to the ordinary CS result \(A_v=-g_mR_D\).

Including channel-length modulation (\(r_o\)) only reduces \(|A_v|\) further; the ideal expression above is the usual design estimate.

### Impedances
- \(R_{\text{in}}\to\infty\) (gate draws no current).
- The resistance seen at the drain is high (\(\sim r_o(1+g_mR_S)+R_S\)), so with \(R_D\) as the only load the voltage gain above is already the loaded gain.

### Role of each element
| Element | Function |
|---|---|
| \(M_1\) (PMOS) | Common-source transconductance; inverting |
| \(R_S\) | Sets \(V_S\) and \(I_D\); degenerates \(g_m\) |
| \(R_D\) | Converts drain current to \(V_{\text{out}}\); sets gain and DC drain level |
| \(V_{DD}\) | Positive supply; AC ground |

- \(M_2\) is a depletion NMOS load (thick channel bar): drain at \(V_{DD}\), gate tied to source at \(V_{\text{out}}\). Thus \(V_{GS2}=0\) always. Because it is depletion mode, \(V_{t2}<0\), so it still conducts at \(V_{GS}=0\).

Use \(k_i=\frac12\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)_i\).

## Qualitative behavior
- \(V_{\text{in}}\) low (\(<V_{t1}\)): \(M_1\) off, no current, so \(V_{\text{out}}=V_{DD}\). The high level is a full rail — the main advantage over an enhancement load.
- \(V_{\text{in}}\) high: \(M_1\) turns on and fights the load. \(M_2\) remains on (\(V_{GS2}=0\)) and, with \(V_{\text{out}}\) low, sits in saturation carrying \(I_D=k_2V_{t2}^2\). \(M_1\) must be made stronger than \(M_2\) to pull \(V_{\text{out}}\) down to a valid low.

## Transfer characteristic
\(M_2\) is saturated for \(V_{\text{out}}\le V_{DD}-|V_{t2}|\) and linear above that; \(M_1\) is off, saturated, or linear as usual.

1. \(V_{\text{in}}<V_{t1}\): \(V_{\text{out}}=V_{DD}\). So \(V_{OH}=V_{DD}\).
2. \(M_1\) saturated, \(M_2\) linear (output still high):
   \[k_1(V_{\text{in}}-V_{t1})^2=k_2\big[2|V_{t2}|(V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}})-(V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}})^2\big].\]
3. Both saturated: with no channel-length modulation the currents match at only one input,
   \[V_{\text{in}}=V_{t1}+|V_{t2}|\sqrt{k_2/k_1},\]
   and the characteristic is vertical there (finite slope once \(\lambda\) is included). This is the high-gain switching region.
4. \(M_1\) linear, \(M_2\) saturated (output low):
   \[k_1\big[2(V_{\text{in}}-V_{t1})V_{\text{out}}-V_{\text{out}}^2\big]=k_2V_{t2}^2.\]

## Output low and required ratio
At \(V_{\text{in}}=V_{DD}\), \(M_2\) is saturated and \(M_1\) linear. For small \(V_{OL}\),
\[V_{OL}\approx\frac{k_2V_{t2}^2}{2k_1(V_{DD}-V_{t1})}.\]
To keep \(V_{OL}\) below the next gate’s threshold, the driver must be stronger than the load:
\[k_R=\frac{k_1}{k_2}=\frac{(W/L)_1}{(W/L)_2}\gtrsim 4.\]
The low level is set by geometry, not restored to ground — hence “ratioed.”

## Power and limitations
Whenever the output is low, the load’s saturation current \(k_2V_{t2}^2\) flows continuously from \(V_{DD}\) to ground, so the gate has static dissipation \(P=V_{DD}\,k_2V_{t2}^2\) in that state. There is no static current when the output is high. That standby power, plus the area cost of the ratioed driver, is why this family was displaced by CMOS. - \(M_1\): gate \(= V_{\text{in}}\), source at ground, drain at the intermediate node \(X\)
- \(M_2\): gate at fixed bias \(V_{b1}\), source at \(X\), drain at \(V_{\text{out}}\)
- \(I_1\): ideal bias from \(V_{DD}\) into the output node

\(V_{\text{in}}\) is a DC bias plus a small signal. \(V_{b1}\) is chosen so both transistors stay in saturation over the intended swing:

\[
V_X \ge V_{\text{in}} - V_{TH1}, \qquad V_{\text{out}} \ge V_{b1} - V_{TH2}
\]

The lowest useful output voltage is set by the two overdrives stacked in series:

\[
V_{\text{out,min}} \approx V_{OV1} + V_{OV2}
\]

That reduced swing is the main cost of the cascode.

## Small-signal behavior

At low frequency the gate of \(M_1\) draws no current, so \(R_{\text{in}} \approx \infty\).

\(M_1\) converts \(v_{\text{in}}\) into a signal current \(g_{m1}v_{\text{in}}\). \(M_2\) passes that current to the output while presenting a low impedance at \(X\) (about \(1/g_{m2}\)) and a very high impedance at the drain. Neglecting body effect and taking \(g_m r_o \gg 1\), the resistance looking into the drain of \(M_2\) is

\[
R_{\text{cas}} \approx g_{m2}\, r_{o1}\, r_{o2}
\]

(with body effect, \(g_{m2}\) becomes \(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}\)). If the current source has finite resistance \(R_I\), the gain is

\[
A_v = \frac{v_{\text{out}}}{v_{\text{in}}} \approx -g_{m1}\,(R_{\text{cas}} \parallel R_I)
\]

With an ideal current source this is on the order of \(-(g_m r_o)^2\), far above the \(-g_{m1}r_{o1}\) of a simple common-source stage. In practice \(R_I\) usually limits the gain, so the cascode’s benefit is realizing a load impedance close to the full \(R_I\) rather than being degraded by \(r_{o1}\).

## Why the cascode is used

- **Gain / \(R_{\text{out}}\):** cascoding multiplies the output resistance by about \(g_{m2}r_{o2}\), so voltage gain rises by that factor when the load is not already the limit.
- **Miller effect:** the gain from \(V_{\text{in}}\) to node \(X\) is only about \(-g_{m1}/g_{m2}\) (often near \(-1\)), not the full stage gain. \(C_{gd1}\) is therefore not multiplied by a large factor, and the input pole moves out.
- **Bandwidth:** the non-dominant pole at \(X\) sits near \(g_{m2}/C_X\), typically well above the output pole. The stage can be faster than a common-source amplifier of the same gain.

## Design constraints

- Size \(M_1\) for the desired \(g_{m1}\) at current \(I_1\); \(M_2\) is often similar or somewhat wider to keep \(V_{OV2}\) small and preserve swing.
- Set \(V_{b1} \approx V_{OV1}+V_{TH1}+V_{GS2}\) so \(M_1\) is just in saturation at the bias point.
- Headroom is \(V_{OV1}+V_{OV2}\) at the bottom and whatever compliance the current source needs at the top.
- Output swing, gain (set by \(R_I \parallel R_{\text{cas}}\)), and the pole at \(X\) are the main tradeoffs.

answer.text:
The circuit is a resistive-load common-source stage whose pull-down is a series stack of two identical NMOS devices with a common gate drive. Under the square-law model it collapses exactly to an ordinary NMOS inverter with half the device strength.

## Topology

- \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are both enhancement NMOS, in series between the output node and ground, with both gates tied to \(V_\text{in}\).
- \(R_D\) is the pull-up to \(V_{DD}\); \(V_\text{out}\) is taken at the drain of \(M_2\).
- The source arrow on each device is at its own source, so each body is tied to its source: \(V_{SB}=0\) and there is no body effect. (If this were an integrated pair with both bodies in a grounded substrate, \(M_2\) would suffer body effect and the equivalence below would not hold.)

## Series-stack equivalence

Assume matched devices, \(k_{n1}=k_{n2}=k_n=\mu_n C_{ox}W/L\), threshold \(V_t\), and neglect channel-length modulation. With the gates tied together and each body at its source, the stack is exactly equivalent to a single NMOS with the same \(V_t\) and

\[
k_{n,\text{eq}}=\frac{k_n}{2}
\]

(i.e. \(W/L\) halved, or \(L\) doubled). Two checks confirm it:

- Both triode (\(V_\text{out}<V_\text{in}-V_t\)): solving the two triode equations for the intermediate source/drain node gives \(I_D=(k_n/2)\big[(V_\text{in}-V_t)V_\text{out}-V_\text{out}^2/2\big]\), which is precisely the triode law of a device with \(k_n/2\).
- Upper device saturated (\(V_\text{out}\ge V_\text{in}-V_t\)): the bottom device is forced into triode, the intermediate voltage settles at \(V_X=(1-1/\sqrt{2})(V_\text{in}-V_t)\approx0.293(V_\text{in}-V_t)\), and \(I_D=(k_n/4)(V_\text{in}-V_t)^2=(1/2)(k_n/2)(V_\text{in}-V_t)^2\), the saturation law of the same equivalent device.

So the circuit is just the classic resistive-load NMOS inverter with pull-down parameter \(k_n/2\). The two transistors can never be in saturation simultaneously: any nonzero current puts \(M_1\) in triode, while \(M_2\) saturates only while \(V_\text{out}\ge V_\text{in}-V_t\).

## Voltage transfer characteristic

With \(V_{OV}=V_\text{in}-V_t\):

1. Cutoff, \(V_\text{in}\le V_t\): \(I_D=0\), so \(V_\text{out}=V_{DD}\). Hence \(V_{OH}=V_{DD}\).

2. Saturation of the equivalent device, \(V_\text{in}>V_t\) and \(V_\text{out}\ge V_\text{in}-V_t\):
\[
I_D=\frac{k_n}{4}(V_\text{in}-V_t)^2,\qquad V_\text{out}=V_{DD}-\frac{k_n R_D}{4}(V_\text{in}-V_t)^2.
\]
This holds up to the boundary \(V_\text{out}=V_\text{in}-V_t\), i.e. up to \(V_\text{in}=V_t+z^\*\) where \(z^\*=2\big[-1+\sqrt{1+k_n R_D V_{DD}}\big]/(k_n R_D)\).

3. Triode, \(V_\text{out}\le V_\text{in}-V_t\):
\[
\frac{V_{DD}-V_\text{out}}{R_D}=\frac{k_n}{2}\Big[(V_\text{in}-V_t)V_\text{out}-\frac{V_\text{out}^2}{2}\Big].
\]

Logic levels from this curve:

- Switching threshold (\(V_\text{in}=V_\text{out}=V_M\)), which falls in the saturation region:
\[
V_M=V_t+\frac{2}{k_n R_D}\Big[-1+\sqrt{1+k_n R_D(V_{DD}-V_t)}\Big].
\]
- \(V_{OL}\) at \(V_\text{in}=V_{DD}\) (triode). For a strong pull-down, neglecting the \(V_{OL}^2\) term,
\[
V_{OL}\approx\frac{V_{DD}}{1+(k_n R_D/2)(V_{DD}-V_t)}.
\]
- The slope is \(-1\) at \(V_{IL}=V_t+2/(k_n R_D)\) (saturation region, provided \(V_{DD}\ge3/(k_n R_D)\)); \(V_{IH}\) is the corresponding slope-\(-1\) point in the triode region. Noise margins are \(NM_L=V_{IL}-V_{OL}\) and \(NM_H=V_{OH}-V_{IH}\).

## Small-signal behavior

Biased in saturation the equivalent device has
\[
g_m=k_{n,\text{eq}}(V_{GS}-V_t)=\frac{k_n}{2}(V_\text{in}-V_t)=\sqrt{k_n I_D},
\]
so with no channel-length modulation the gain is
\[
A_v=-g_m R_D=-\frac{k_n R_D}{2}(V_\text{in}-V_t).
\]
The stage must be biased with \(V_\text{out}>V_\text{in}-V_t\) to stay in this high-gain region. Including \(\lambda\), stacking raises the effective output resistance of the pull-down, but the gain is still set by \(R_D\) unless \(R_D\) approaches that resistance.

## Summary

Functionally it is an inverting common-source stage: \(V_\text{out}=V_{DD}\) for \(V_\text{in}<V_t\) and falls toward a small \(V_{OL}\) as \(V_\text{in}\) rises. The gate-tied series stack does not change the shape of the characteristic relative to a single driver; it only halves \(k_n\), which weakens the pull-down, raises \(V_{OL}\), shifts \(V_M\), and halves \(g_m\) (and therefore the gain) compared with one device of parameter \(k_n\).

answer.text:
The circuit is an NMOS source-coupled differential pair with a single-ended resistive load. \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) share a tail current sink \(I_1\); \(V_{in}\) drives \(M_1\), \(V_b\) is a DC reference on \(M_2\), and \(V_{out}\) is taken only from \(M_2\)’s drain. \(M_1\)’s drain is tied to \(V_{DD}\) and does not set the output.

### Large-signal behavior
The tail enforces
\[
I_{D1}+I_{D2}=I_1.
\]
With matched devices and \(V_{in}=V_b\), the pair is balanced:
\[
I_{D1}=I_{D2}=\frac{I_1}{2},\qquad V_{out}=V_{DD}-\frac{I_1}{2}R_D.
\]
Raising \(V_{in}\) above \(V_b\) steers current into \(M_1\) and out of \(M_2\), so the drop on \(R_D\) falls and \(V_{out}\) rises. The transfer is therefore non-inverting. Both devices conduct only for
\[
|V_{in}-V_b|<\sqrt{2}\,V_{OV},
\]
where \(V_{OV}=V_{GS}-V_t\) is the equilibrium overdrive at \(I_D=I_1/2\). Outside that window the pair is fully steered: \(V_{out}\to V_{DD}\) if \(V_{in}\gg V_b\), and \(V_{out}\to V_{DD}-I_1 R_D\) if \(V_{in}\ll V_b\).

### Small-signal gain
With \(V_b\) an AC ground and an ideal tail source, the source node sits at \(v_{in}/2\). Then
\[
i_{d2}=-\frac{g_m}{2}v_{in},\qquad A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=\frac{g_m R_D}{2},
\]
where \(g_m\) is evaluated at \(I_D=I_1/2\). Body effect does not change this result: it raises the effective transconductance of both devices equally and cancels at the coupled sources. Finite \(r_o\) lowers the gain slightly and makes
\[
R_{out}\approx R_D\parallel r_{o2}
\]
(plus a weak contribution from the source network).

### Bias constraints
- Both MOSFETs must stay in saturation: \(V_{DS}>V_{OV}\). That is automatic for \(M_1\) (\(V_D=V_{DD}\)), but \(V_{out}\) must remain above \(V_S+V_{OV2}\).
- The tail source needs compliance: \(V_S=V_b-V_{GS2}\) must stay high enough for \(I_1\) to remain a stiff sink.
- Because \(V_{DS1}\neq V_{DS2}\), channel-length modulation unbalances the quiescent currents and creates a systematic offset that a symmetric or current-mirror load would avoid.

### Practical limitations
- Gain is half that of a fully differential resistively loaded pair, since only one drain current is converted to voltage.
- Supply gain is about 1: \(V_{DD}\) noise appears directly at \(V_{out}\), so PSRR is poor.
- Common-mode rejection of a disturbance common to \(V_{in}\) and \(V_b\) is high only while \(I_1\) is an ideal current source; a real tail impedance sets the CMRR.

- \(M_1\): gate at node \(X\), drain at the \(V_{out}\) node, source at ground. With \(R_{D1}\) it is a common-source stage loaded by \(R_{D1}\).
- \(M_2\): gate at \(V_{out}\), drain at node \(X\), source at ground — a second common-source stage.
- \(I_{in}\) (arrow upward) injects current into node \(X\); \(M_2\) is the only path that can remove it. So in any DC state, \(I_{D2}=I_{in}\).
- \(V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_{D1}R_{D1}\), since \(M_2\)'s gate draws no current.

KCL at \(X\) forces \(I_{D2}=I_{in}\), which suggests the equilibrium
\[
V_{out}=V_{th2}+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{in}}{\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)_2}},
\]
with \(V_X=V_{GS1}\) then set by \(I_{D1}=(V_{DD}-V_{out})/R_{D1}\). But the loop around it is regenerative. Breaking the loop at \(M_2\)'s gate and injecting \(v_t\):

\[
\frac{v_x}{v_t}=-g_{m2}r_{o2},\qquad \frac{v_{out}}{v_x}=-g_{m1}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}),
\]

so the loop gain is
\[
T=g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})\;\gg\;1
\]
and **positive** (two common-source inversions). The equilibrium is unstable and the circuit rails.

## Stable state

The only self-consistent bounded state is the upper rail:

- \(M_1\) off \(\Rightarrow I_{D1}=0\Rightarrow V_{out}=V_{DD}\).
- \(M_2\) then has \(V_{GS}=V_{DD}\) and operates in deep triode, absorbing \(I_{in}\) at a small drain voltage:
\[
V_X\approx\frac{I_{in}}{\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)_2\,(V_{DD}-V_{th2})}.
\]
- This holds as long as \(V_X<V_{th1}\), i.e.
\[
I_{in}<V_{th1}\,\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)_2\,(V_{DD}-V_{th2}),
\]
which is satisfied for any ordinary bias current, so \(M_1\) indeed stays cut off.

The opposite rail (\(V_{out}\) low, \(M_2\) off) is not a bounded state with an ideal current source: with \(M_2\) off, \(I_{in}\) has nowhere to leave node \(X\), so \(V_X\) climbs without limit. Only the finite compliance of a real current source would cap it, creating a second, compliance-limited state. With the ideal elements drawn, the circuit settles at \(V_{out}=V_{DD}\), \(M_1\) cut off, \(M_2\) in triode.

answer.text:
The circuit is a cross-coupled NMOS pair — a regenerative (positive-feedback) bistable cell, i.e. a current-driven latch / Schmitt trigger — not a linear amplifier.

## Connections

- \(M_1\): gate = node \(X\), drain = \(V_{out}\), source = ground, drain load \(R_{D1}\) to \(V_{DD}\).
- \(M_2\): drain = node \(X\), gate = \(V_{out}\), source = ground.
- \(I_{in}\) injects current into node \(X\).

So each gate is tied to the other device’s drain: \(V_{G1}=V_{D2}=V_X\) and \(V_{G2}=V_{D1}=V_{out}\). Both sources are grounded, so \(V_{SB}=0\) (no body effect).

## KCL constraints (always true at DC)

Since the gates draw no current:

\[
I_{D2}=I_{in}, \qquad I_{D1}=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D1}}.
\]

## Feedback polarity — the interior bias point is unstable

Each transistor is a common-source stage, so each contributes one inversion. Two inversions in the loop make the feedback **positive**. Linearizing about a point where both devices are in saturation (small-signal parameters \(g_{m1},r_{o1},g_{m2},r_{o2}\), with \(R_L=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}\)):

\[
C_X\dot v_X=i_{in}-g_{m2}v_{out}-\frac{v_X}{r_{o2}}, \qquad C_o\dot v_{out}=-g_{m1}v_X-\frac{v_{out}}{R_L}.
\]

The Jacobian has a negative trace but a **negative determinant**,

\[
\det J \propto \frac{1}{r_{o2}R_L}-g_{m1}g_{m2}<0,
\]

because the loop gain

\[
T = g_{m1}R_L\cdot g_{m2}r_{o2}
\]

is positive and \(\gg 1\). A negative determinant means one positive real eigenvalue: the equilibrium is a saddle. Equivalently, breaking the loop at \(M_2\)’s gate and driving it with \(v_s\) (\(i_{in}=0\)) returns

\[
\frac{v_{out}}{v_s}=+g_{m1}g_{m2}R_L r_{o2}\gg +1.
\]

So the circuit regenerates; it will not sit at the simultaneous-saturation point.

That unstable point, for reference only, would be (square law, \(I_D=\tfrac{\beta}{2}(V_{GS}-V_t)^2\), \(\beta=\mu_n C_{ox}W/L\))

\[
V_{out}=V_t+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{in}}{\beta_2}},\qquad V_X=V_t+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{D1}}{\beta_1}},
\]

and the apparent small-signal slope \(v_{out}/i_{in}\approx 1/g_{m2}\) is only the slope **at this unstable point** — it is not a usable gain.

## Bistable behavior

Regeneration drives the circuit to a rail state where the loop is broken (a device off or in deep triode, so \(T<1\)) and it latches. Because \(M_2\) must carry \(I_{in}\), \(V_{out}>V_t\) in every DC state.

- **High state** (\(M_1\) cut off): \(V_{out}=V_{DD}\), \(M_2\) in triode carrying \(I_{in}\) with \(V_{GS2}=V_{DD}\) and \(V_X\le V_t\). It exists only while \(M_2\) can pass \(I_{in}\) at \(V_{DS2}\le V_t\):

\[
I_{in}\le I_{\text{crit,H}}=\beta_2\!\left[(V_{DD}-V_t)V_t-\frac{V_t^2}{2}\right].
\]

  It is stable because \(M_1\) is off (\(g_{m1}=0\)), so the loop gain is zero.

- **Low state** (\(M_1\) on, triode): \(M_1\) pulls \(V_{out}\) down and \(M_2\), gated by that low \(V_{out}\), still carries \(I_{in}\). \(M_1\) in triode keeps the loop gain below 1, so this state is stable. It exists only above a lower critical current \(I_{\text{crit,L}}\).

For \(I_{\text{crit,L}}<I_{in}<I_{\text{crit,H}}\) both states exist, so the \(V_{out}\) vs. \(I_{in}\) characteristic has **hysteresis**. Crossing \(I_{\text{crit,H}}\) upward turns \(M_1\) on and the positive feedback snaps the cell to the low state; falling below \(I_{\text{crit,L}}\) snaps it back to the high state.

Assumptions: saturation, no body effect, \(r_o\to\infty\), no capacitances (midband).

Let \(v_s\) be the source voltage of \(M_1\) and \(G=g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}\). Nodal analysis gives

\[

\[
\frac{V_\mathrm{out}}{I_\mathrm{in}}
=-\frac{R_{D2}(G R_F-1)}{G R_{D2}+g_{m1}(R_F+R_{D2})+1}.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\frac{V_\mathrm{out}}{I_\mathrm{in}}
=-\frac{(g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_F-1)R_{D2}}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}+g_{m1}(R_F+R_{D2})+1}.

\[
\frac{V_\mathrm{out}}{I_\mathrm{in}}\approx -R_F.
\]

That is the design equation for the TIA: the closed-loop transimpedance is set by the feedback resistor, not by the transistor parameters.

- \(g_{m2}\to\infty\) forces \(v_s\to 0\), so \(V_\mathrm{out}=-I_\mathrm{in}R_F\).
- \(R_F\to\infty\) (feedback removed) leaves the open-loop transimpedance \(-g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}\). The \(g_{m1}\) cancels: \(M_1\) converts \(I_\mathrm{in}\) into \(v_X=I_\mathrm{in}R_{D1}\), and \(M_2\) amplifies that voltage by \(-g_{m2}R_{D2}\).

\[
Z_\mathrm{in}=\frac{v_s}{I_\mathrm{in}}

- With high loop gain,

\]

| Element | Role |
|---|---|
| \(M_1\) (CG) | Current buffer; sets a moderately low \(Z_\mathrm{in}\) even before feedback; \(R_{D1}\) converts its current to the voltage at \(X\) |
| \(M_2\) (CS) | Inverting voltage gain that makes the loop gain large and sets the sign of the feedback |
| \(R_F\) | Sets \(V_\mathrm{out}/I_\mathrm{in}\approx -R_F\); also closes the DC bias loop |
| \(R_{D1}, R_{D2}\) | Loads; their product with the transconductances sets loop gain (and therefore how closely the gain approaches \(-R_F\) and how low \(Z_\mathrm{in}\) becomes) |
| \(V_b\) | Bias for \(M_1\); together with \(R_{D1}\) it places \(M_2\) in saturation |

- Loop gain must stay large over the intended signal range, otherwise the gain falls below \(R_F\) and becomes sensitive to \(g_m\) and the drain resistors (see the exact expression).

Bandwidth is then set by the loop gain and the poles at \(X\) and \(V_\mathrm{out}\), not by \(R_F C_\mathrm{in}\) alone. No capacitors are shown, so that is outside the midband model above.
- Noise of \(R_F\) appears directly at the output as a current noise \(4kT/R_F\) referred to the input; raising \(R_F\) improves both gain and noise but costs loop gain and bandwidth.

**Bottom line:** it is a CG–CS shunt-feedback TIA whose midband transimpedance is \(-R_F\) when the loop gain is high, with a feedback-suppressed input impedance well below \(1/g_{m1}\).

answers.question: Analyze the arrangement in the figure.

answer.text:
The figure shows a single closed loop of three inverters with two series switches controlled by complementary clocks, \(CK\) and \(\overline{CK}\). The output of the last inverter is fed back to the input of the \(CK\) switch.

**Inversion parity.** Three inverters make the loop inverting overall. A continuously closed loop with an odd number of inversions has no stable state and would free-run as a ring oscillator, with a period of about six inverter delays.

**The switches prevent free-running.** Assuming a switch conducts when its control is high, \(CK\) and \(\overline{CK}\) are never high at the same time. In one phase only the left switch conducts; in the other only the \(\overline{CK}\) switch conducts. The regenerative loop is therefore broken in both phases, so the circuit does not oscillate on its own.

**What it does instead.** Each open switch leaves the following inverter input floating, so that node holds its value dynamically as stored charge. Tracing the two phases:

- \(CK=1\): the feedback value is sampled onto Inv1 and inverted, while the downstream pair holds.
- \(CK=0\): Inv1’s result is released into the two-inverter pair, and that value propagates back to the feedback node.

Because Inv1 has already inverted the sampled value, the feedback node returns inverted. It therefore toggles once per clock cycle and repeats only every two cycles — a divide-by-2, i.e. a toggle (T) flip-flop function, paced by the clock rather than by gate delay.

**Caveats.** Operation is dynamic: the clock must be fast enough that leakage does not corrupt the floating nodes, and those nodes float every phase, so a slow or stopped clock leaves inverter inputs undefined. Non-overlapping phases are preferable; if \(CK\) and \(\overline{CK}\) overlap, both switches conduct briefly, the odd loop closes momentarily, and a runt pulse or burst of ring oscillation can occur.

- \(CK=1\), \(\overline{CK}=0\): feedback reaches \(\mathrm{Inv}_1\), but \(\mathrm{Inv}_1\)’s output is cut off from the rest of the chain.
- \(CK=0\), \(\overline{CK}=1\): \(\mathrm{Inv}_1\) can drive the following inverters, but the feedback into \(\mathrm{Inv}_1\) is open.

There is therefore no continuous regenerative path, and the circuit does not oscillate the way an ungated three-inverter ring would.

**What the nodes do instead.** While a switch is open, the node on its far side is floating and only holds its last voltage on capacitance (dynamic storage). Each phase moves or isolates charge; it does not sustain a running oscillation. Leakage will eventually corrupt those floating levels if a phase is held too long.

**Edge cases.** A long overlap in which both switches conduct can briefly close the odd-inversion loop and produce a runt pulse or a short burst, not stable periodic oscillation. If both switches were gated by the same clock, the loop would oscillate whenever that clock was high.

- Signal path: feedback node → \(CK\) switch → Inv₁ → \(\overline{CK}\) switch → inverter → inverter → back to the feedback node.

Tracing one full clock cycle, the value stored at Inv₁’s input is returned through three inversions, so it is inverted once per clock period. Every node therefore toggles once per clock cycle.

The circuit divides the clock by 2: the oscillating nodes run at \(f_{CK}/2\). It relies on complementary, non-overlapping switch conduction and on the clock being fast enough that stored charge is not lost between phases. If both switches conducted at once, the odd loop would be closed and the inverters would fight; proper complementary clocking avoids that.

answers.question: If the LDO regulator in the figure generates thermal noise with spectrum Sth, how do we compute the VCO output phase noise?

answer.text:
The LDO thermal noise appears directly as a voltage disturbance on \(V_\text{out}\). Because the tank inductors force the common-mode level of the oscillation nodes to equal \(V_\text{out}\), this disturbance changes the bias voltage that appears across the varactors by exactly the same amount. Consequently the oscillation frequency is modulated with a sensitivity equal to the supply-pushing factor
\[
K_\text{push}=\frac{\partial f_\text{osc}}{\partial V_\text{out}}
\]
(identical in magnitude to the ordinary tuning gain \(K_\text{VCO}\) when the only voltage-dependent capacitances are the varactors).

A voltage-noise spectrum \(S_\text{th}(\Delta f)\) therefore produces a frequency-noise spectrum \(K_\text{push}^2S_\text{th}(\Delta f)\). Integration of frequency into phase yields the one-sided phase spectral density \(S_\theta(\Delta f)=K_\text{push}^2S_\text{th}(\Delta f)/(\Delta f)^2\). The corresponding single-sideband phase noise is
\[
\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)=10\log_{10}\Biggl(\frac{K_\text{push}^2S_\text{th}(\Delta f)}{2(\Delta f)^2}\Biggr).
\]
(The same result is obtained by a full periodic-noise simulation once the LDO noise source has been annotated with spectrum \(S_\text{th}\); the analytic expression above simply makes the dominant conversion mechanism explicit.)

Final answer: \(\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)=10\log_{10}[K_\text{push}^{2}S_\text{th}(\Delta f)/(2(\Delta f)^{2})]\)

answers.question: If the LDO regulator in the figure generates thermal noise with spectrum Sth, how do we compute the VCO output phase noise?

answer.text:
The LDO thermal noise appears directly as a voltage disturbance on the VCO supply node \(V_\text{out}\). Denote the PSD of this disturbance by \(S_\text{th}(f)\) (V\(^2\)/Hz).

Because the tank common-mode level sits at \(V_\text{out}\), the same disturbance modulates every voltage-dependent capacitance in the tank (most importantly the varactors, but also the bias-dependent device capacitances of \(M_1\)-\(M_2\)). The net result is a fluctuation of the oscillation frequency whose sensitivity is the supply pushing factor
\[
K_\text{push}=\frac{\partial f_\text{osc}}{\partial V_\text{out}}
\]
(Hz/V). (When varactor modulation dominates, \(|K_\text{push}|\approx K_\text{VCO}\), but the equality is not required for the derivation.)

Frequency noise is therefore related to supply noise by
\[
S_{\Delta f}(f)=K_\text{push}^2\,S_\text{th}(f).
\]
Phase is the integral of excess frequency, which multiplies the PSD by \(1/f^2\):
\[
S_\phi(f)=\frac{K_\text{push}^2\,S_\text{th}(f)}{f^2}.
\]
The single-sideband phase-noise spectrum that is normally quoted for the VCO output then follows at once:
\[
\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)=10\log_{10}\Biggl(\frac{K_\text{push}^2\,S_\text{th}(\Delta f)}{2(\Delta f)^2}\Biggr)
\quad\text{(dBc/Hz)}.
\]
(The quasi-static pushing model used above is accurate for all offset frequencies of practical interest, because an LDO’s output noise is band-limited to well below the carrier.)

Final answer: \(\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)=10\log_{10}[K_{push}^{2}S_{th}(\Delta f)/(2(\Delta f)^{2})]\)

answer.text:
The addition of \(C_T\) has two opposing effects, so the net change in phase noise depends on its value (and on the oscillation amplitude).

- Noise of \(I_{SS}\) near \(2f_0\) is mixed into phase noise around the carrier. A moderate \(C_T\) shunts that noise to ground and therefore lowers phase noise.

Consequently an optimum \(C_T\) exists; a capacitor that is either too small or too large leaves the phase noise higher than this optimum. (The classic remedy that obtains both noise filtering and a high impedance at \(2f_0\) is a series inductor between the common-source node and the parallel combination of \(I_{SS}\) and \(C_T\).)
